title: Can varargs (`String... args`) replace `String[] args` in the `main` method?
shortTitle: Can varargs replace String[] args in the main method?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. Declaring main as public static void main of a String varargs is fully accepted by the Java Virtual Machine as the application entry point, because varargs is compiled to exactly the same signature as a String array. At the bytecode level there is no difference between a String varargs parameter and a String array parameter; the only distinction is a compiler flag that marks the method as varargs so it can auto-bundle arguments at call sites. Since the JVM launcher resolves the entry point by the erased signature, which is identical for both forms, the varargs version starts the program just like the array version. The command-line arguments still arrive as a String array inside the method.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the official opening-time front door must be of one exact standard shape so head office can recognize it. Writing the door as a String array is like building that standard door one way, and writing it as String varargs is like building the very same standard door with a slightly different label on the blueprint, but once installed the two doors are physically identical. Head office, meaning the JVM, measures the installed door, finds it is exactly the standard shape, and opens the branch through it without caring which blueprint label was used. So the branch opens the same either way, and the instruction slip, meaning the arguments, still arrives as the same bundle inside.
s1_definition.oneliner: Yes, String varargs works as the main entry point because it compiles to the identical String array signature the JVM looks for, and the arguments still arrive as a String array.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. Declaring main as public static void main of a String varargs is fully accepted by the Java Virtual Machine as the application entry point, because varargs is compiled to exactly the same signature as a String array. At the bytecode level there is no difference between a String varargs parameter and a String array parameter; the only distinction is a compiler flag that marks the method as varargs so it can auto-bundle arguments at call sites. Since the JVM launcher resolves the entry point by the erased signature, which is identical for both forms, the varargs version starts the program just like the array version. The command-line arguments still arrive as a String array inside the method.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the official opening-time front door must be of one exact standard shape so head office can recognize it. Writing the door as a String array is like building that standard door one way, and writing it as String varargs is like building the very same standard door with a slightly different label on the blueprint, but once installed the two doors are physically identical. Head office, meaning the JVM, measures the installed door, finds it is exactly the standard shape, and opens the branch through it without caring which blueprint label was used. So the branch opens the same either way, and the instruction slip, meaning the arguments, still arrives as the same bundle inside.

**One line to remember:** Yes, String varargs works as the main entry point because it compiles to the identical String array signature the JVM looks for, and the arguments still arrive as a String array.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason this works is erasure of the varargs syntax to an array. When you declare a parameter as String with an ellipsis, the compiler produces a method whose parameter type is a String array, and it sets a flag indicating the method is varargs. The flag only affects how callers may invoke the method, allowing loose arguments to be auto-bundled; it does not change the parameter type. So public static void main of a String varargs and public static void main of a String array have the same descriptor as far as the class file and the JVM are concerned.

The JVM launcher looks up the entry point by that descriptor: it needs a public static method named main, returning void, taking a single String array parameter. Because the varargs form produces exactly that descriptor, the launcher finds it and invokes it. The arguments the user typed on the command line are passed in as the elements of the array, so inside the method the parameter behaves identically whether you wrote it as varargs or as an array; you index into it and read its length the same way.

There is no behavioral difference at runtime. Reading args at index zero, iterating over args, and checking args length all work the same. The empty case is also the same: with no command-line arguments the array has length zero and is never null.

Several senior points matter. First, although it is legal, the overwhelming convention is to write the main parameter as a String array, because that is what every reader expects and it signals the entry point clearly; using varargs for main is a curiosity that can momentarily confuse readers, so most teams keep the array form. Second, because the two forms have the same erased signature, you cannot declare both in the same class as if they were overloads; they would collide as a duplicate method. Third, the varargs form does give you the minor convenience that if you call main yourself from other code, you could pass loose string arguments without building an array, which is occasionally handy in tests, but that is a small benefit. Fourth, the parameter name args is only a convention in either form and can be any identifier. In banking code the practical guidance is that the varargs main is valid and harmless, but I keep the conventional String array form for the entry point to maximize clarity, reserving varargs for ordinary methods where the flexible argument count is genuinely useful.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer wrote the settlement launcher's main with String varargs and wondered whether the JVM would still start it. This is exactly the question of whether varargs can serve as the entry point.

Problem 2 — The team wanted to confirm the command-line arguments still arrive correctly and that the empty case is safe. This is exactly verifying the identical runtime behavior and the empty-not-null rule.

Problem 3 — The team also noticed a small testing convenience: calling the varargs main directly with loose strings without building an array. This is exactly the minor varargs benefit at call sites.

The code provides a `VarargsMainDemo` class whose entry point is declared with String varargs, reads the arguments exactly like an array, and includes a small internal call passing loose arguments to show the convenience, all for a Rajesh settlement.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
varargs-main-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/batch/
│       └── VarargsMainDemo.java   (entry point declared as String... args)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/batch/VarargsMainDemo.java

# Run with no arguments → defaults, then self-call with loose varargs
java -cp out com.bank.batch.VarargsMainDemo

# Run with command-line arguments → arrive as args[0], args[1]
java -cp out com.bank.batch.VarargsMainDemo CUR3001 75000.00

# Prove the erased signature is String[]:
javap -p -c out/com/bank/batch/VarargsMainDemo.class | grep main
# shows: public static void main(java.lang.String[]);   (with a varargs flag)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: either no command-line arguments or the two words CUR3001 and 75000.00.

Step 1 — The entry point is declared with String varargs, which the compiler erases to a String array parameter with a varargs flag. The resulting method descriptor is identical to the conventional array form, so the JVM launcher recognizes it as the valid entry point.

Step 2 — When run with no arguments, the launcher passes an empty String array of length zero, not null, to the method. The code reads the defaults, Rajesh's account and fifty thousand, exactly as it would with an array parameter.

Step 3 — Because no arguments were supplied, the code demonstrates the small varargs convenience by calling main itself with two loose string arguments. The compiler automatically bundles those into a new String array, so the self-call runs as if two command-line arguments had been passed.

Step 4 — On that self-call, the method reads CUR3001 and seventy five thousand from the array and logs the settlement, showing identical behavior to a real command-line invocation.

Step 5 — When run with actual command-line arguments, the launcher bundles CUR3001 and 75000.00 into the array, and the method reads them at indices zero and one, settling seventy five thousand for CUR3001, proving the arguments arrive the same as with the array form.

Step 6 — Inspecting the compiled class with javap confirms the parameter type is a String array, demonstrating that varargs and array are the same at the bytecode level and thus both valid entry points.

```
# java VarargsMainDemo
Oct 30, 2026 5:35:12 PM com.bank.batch.VarargsMainDemo main
INFO: Entry via String... args — arg count = 0
INFO: Settling Rs.50000.00 for account SAV2001
INFO: Re-invoking main with loose varargs arguments (test-style call):
INFO: Entry via String... args — arg count = 2
INFO: Settling Rs.75000.00 for account CUR3001

# javap output
  public static void main(java.lang.String[]);
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Source: public static void main(String... args)
    │ compiler erases varargs → array (+ varargs flag)
    ▼
  Class file descriptor: main([Ljava/lang/String;)V   ← identical to String[] form
    │
    ▼
  JVM launcher: matches entry point signature → invokes main
    │
    ├─ java VarargsMainDemo            → args = String[0]  → defaults
    │       │ self-call main("CUR3001","75000.00") → compiler bundles → String[2]
    │       ▼
    │     settle Rs.75000 for CUR3001
    │
    └─ java VarargsMainDemo CUR3001 75000.00 → args = String[]{"CUR3001","75000.00"}
            ▼
          settle Rs.75000 for CUR3001

  Conclusion: String... args ≡ String[] args as the entry point.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, a main declared with String varargs works perfectly well as the application entry point, and the reason is that varargs is nothing more than array syntax at the source level. When I write the main parameter as String with an ellipsis, the compiler erases that to a String array parameter and sets a flag marking the method as varargs. The resulting method descriptor in the class file is byte-for-byte the same as if I had written a String array, and the varargs flag only affects how callers may invoke the method, not its type.

The JVM launcher resolves the entry point purely by that descriptor: it looks for a public static method named main, returning void, taking one String array parameter. Because the varargs form produces exactly that descriptor, the launcher finds it and starts the program just as it would with the array form. Inside the method the command-line arguments arrive as the elements of the array, so indexing, reading the length, and the empty-not-null behavior are all identical. There is simply no runtime difference.

That said, the convention I follow and recommend is to keep the main parameter as a String array, because that is the form every Java developer instantly recognizes as the entry point, and writing it as varargs is a small curiosity that can momentarily confuse a reader. In our banking launchers I keep the conventional array form for clarity and reserve varargs for ordinary methods where a genuinely variable argument count is useful, like an audit method or a totaling utility.

The senior points I add are these. Because the two forms have the identical erased signature, I cannot declare both a String array main and a String varargs main in the same class; they would collide as a duplicate method rather than being overloads. The one minor benefit of the varargs form is that if I call main myself from other code, such as in a test, I can pass loose string arguments without building an array, and the compiler bundles them for me. And the parameter name args is only a convention in either form. So my answer is a confident yes, it is valid and behaves identically, backed by the fact that varargs compiles to a String array, while my practical preference stays with the conventional array form for readability.

---

keyPoints: Yes — main(String... args) is identical to main(String[] args)
Varargs is syntactic sugar for an array parameter
JVM accepts both signatures as the entry point
Internally compiled to the same bytecode
